newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan PM gets royal support for economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Jordan PM gets royal support for economic reform.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan has signalled he is ready to give Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti a long-term mandate for wide-ranging economic and administrative reforms.

The official Petra news agency quoted the king, who in the past has favoured reshuffling prime ministers on a regular basis, as saying he had discussed with Kabariti a political programme extending beyond elections set for November.

"I said to him if he still had the same enthusiasm, honesty, bravery, integrity and righteousness which we know he has...we will look at future issues with a new style," Petra quoted King Hussein as saying in a television interview late on Friday.
"But if he is scared of confronting storms...and I do not think that is the case, then we will have to think of another solution," he added.
Kabariti, in Gaza to meet Palestinian Authority President Yasser Arafat on Saturday, was not available to comment.
But a government official said the king's comments reflected a "renewal of confidence" in Kabariti's one-year-old government and a call to accelerate reforms.

"The statement reflects the political will of the leadership to carry out whatever measures are needed in the way of reform and to meet challenges head-on," said the official, who asked not to be named.

Since his appointment in February last year Kabariti has pushed ahead with IMF-backed economic reforms, including a cut in bread subsidies which led to riots in southern Jordan last August and opposition demands for his resignation.
His government has also tabled legislation to reform laws covering company finances, customs duties, the Amman stock exchange and parliamentary elections.

But King Hussein said Jordan must take more steps in its battle against "deadly bureaucracy". After visiting a government department with Kabariti recently, "we left with the impression that this department would have been more productive if 70 percent of it were cut back," he said.
The king had been expected to announce within weeks a temporary government to lead Jordan into the November election.
Under Jordanian law, ministers serving in cabinet cannot stand for a parliamentary seat. Two thirds of the cabinet are members of parliament and some plan to run for parliament again.

But the king hinted that in future parliamentarians may be kept out of the cabinet, splitting the government's legislative and executive branches, and said he was looking beyond the few months leading up to the elections.
"The next stage will not only be an interim phase for holding the elections," he said.

"Plenty of evidence shows that it is not right to combine deputies and ministers (roles)," he added. "The deputy is a monitor of the government and he should devote his time and effort to following up the different laws put before them."

Critics of the present system say it almost guarantees the government a majority in the 80-seat lower house of parliament because a quarter of deputies are also ministers. Other deputies support the government in the hope of winning a cabinet post at the next reshuffle, they say.

King Hussein also criticised Islamist MPs who walked out of parliament last week in protest at what they said was a weak government reaction to Israeli plans to build Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem.
"I don't think that deputies were elected just to withdraw from parliament every now and then," he said.
